claims.source: With the polarizer removed, PSI values in DmDRA1 neurons fell by approximately 80% (Figure 1E,F), reflecting their lack of modulation and resulting in an average ΔPSI of 0.59, whereas PSI values in the background showed no change (Figure 1F), resulting in an average ΔPSI of 0.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the control experiment data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: Within the population of DmDRA1 neurons, the preferred angle of polarization shows a linear relationship with position, which is referred to as polarotopy.
claims.source: Within the population of DmDRA1 neurons, we observed preferential responses to different angles of polarized light depending on their position in the MEDRA (Figure 1C,G). The preferred AoP showed a linear relationship with position, which we refer to as polarotopy (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of tuning data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claims.claim: Moving anterior to posterior in the right optic lobe, the preferred angle of polarization in DmDRA1 neurons shifts counter-clockwise.
claims.source: Moving anterior to posterior in the right optic lobe, the preferred AoP shifted counter-clockwise (Figure 1G,H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the polarotopy analysis shown in Figure 1G,H.

claims.claim: The polarotopy in the left optic lobe is mirrored compared to the right optic lobe, with a similar range of preferred angles of polarization represented in the opposite posterior-anterior direction.
claims.source: This polarotopy was mirrored in the left optic lobe, with a similar range of preferred AoPs represented in the opposite posterior-anterior direction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: The preferred angles of polarization of DmDRA1 neurons closely match those of R8 photoreceptors at similar positions.
claims.source: Throughout the MEDRA, the preferred AoPs of DmDRA1 neurons closely matched those of R8 photoreceptors at similar positions (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of tuning data from DmDRA1 and R8 shown in the figures.

claims.claim: R7/R8 photoreceptors are likely inhibitory.
claims.source: Since R7/R8 are likely inhibitory (Davis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2008), we expected that the preferred AoP of a neuron postsynaptic to either R7 or R8 would be shifted by 90°.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on photoreceptor signaling.

claims.claim: R7 signals are responsible for the predominant response characteristics of DmDRA1 neurons.
claims.source: We therefore posit that it is R7 signals that are responsible for the predominant response characteristics of DmDRA1 neurons, consistent with the anatomical overlap between DmDRA1 and R7 terminals (Figure 1B'') and the established connectivity of the DmDRA1 subtype (Sancer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the tuning data, anatomical data, and cited connectivity information.

claims.claim: DmDRA1 neurons show polarization opponency, with activity increases at preferred angles and inhibition at anti-preferred angles.
claims.source: The preferred AoP of 0° caused an increase in activity relative to baseline, while flashes at 90° caused a decrease of greater magnitude, followed by a slight rebound above baseline after the offset of the flash (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flash response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: DmDRA1 neurons are inhibited by unpolarized light regardless of position in the MEDRA.
claims.source: For light flashes with the polarizer removed we observed inhibition of DmDRA1 at all regions, regardless of position in the MEDRA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the control experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The excitation of DmDRA1 neurons by preferred angles of polarization is likely a release from R7-mediated inhibition.
claims.source: This excitation is likely to be a release from R7-mediated inhibition, with R7 and DmDRA1 tuned to orthogonal angles of polarization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the response properties and known inhibitory nature of R7.

claims.claim: In other insect species, polarization-sensitive photoreceptors in the dorsal rim are thought to provide input to transmedulla neurons.
claims.source: In other insect species, polarization-sensitive photoreceptors in the dorsal rim are thought to provide input to transmedulla neurons (also referred to as line-tangential neurons), which project from the optic lobe to the anterior optic tubercle (AOTU) (el Jundi et al., 2011; Homberg et al., 2003; Immonen et al., 2017; Pfeiffer and Kinoshita, 2012; Zeller et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research in other insect species.

claims.claim: In all insect species investigated, the small subunit of the AOTU is involved in processing polarized light signals.
claims.source: In all species investigated, it is the small subunit of the AOTU (often called the lower-unit, LU) which is involved in processing polarized light signals (Heinze, 2013), although to our knowledge these signals have not been explored in transmedulla neurons themselves.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review and notes a gap in knowledge.

claims.claim: Individual MeTu neurons typically innervate 10–15 columns of the medulla in layers M6–7.
claims.source: The dendrites of individual MeTu neurons typically innervate 10–15 columns of the medulla in layers M6–7 (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and, as an ensemble, tile larger areas of the medulla (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical characterization and the figure.

claims.claim: MeTu neurons as an ensemble tile larger areas of the medulla.
claims.source: The dendrites of individual MeTu neurons typically innervate 10–15 columns of the medulla in layers M6–7 (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and, as an ensemble, tile larger areas of the medulla (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Trans-Tango labeling from DmDRA1-split identified a population of neurons in the dorsal medulla that project to the small, lateral subunit of the AOTU via the anterior optic tract.
claims.source: We found that DmDRA1-split driving trans-Tango labeled a population of neurons in the dorsal medulla that project to the small, lateral subunit of the AOTU via a fiber bundle in the anterior optic tract (AOT) (Figure 2B), and matched the anatomy of MeTu neurons (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango tracing data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Trans-Tango labeling from Rh3/Rh4-Gal4 identified labeling of the small subunit of the AOTU.
claims.source: We again found trans-Tango labeling of the small subunit of the AOTU (Figure 2C), indicating connectivity between UV-sensitive photoreceptors and MeTu neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: MeTu dendrites are in close proximity to DRA R7 terminals in layer M6 of the dorsal medulla.
claims.source: Throughout layer M6 in the dorsal medulla, MeTu dendrites were in close proximity to non-DRA R7 terminals and at the dorsal-posterior margin we found clear overlap with DRA R7 terminals, distinguishable by their larger terminals and deeper projections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: At least some MeTu neurons appear to receive input from DRA R7 photoreceptors.
claims.source: In short, at least some MeTu neurons appear to receive input from DRA R7 photoreceptors (in addition to non-DRA photoreceptors and possibly DRA R8) and the putative connections revealed here suggest a parallel pathway for polarization signals in the MEDRA: DRA R7→DmDRA1, DmDRA1→MeTu, DRA R7→MeTu (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the anatomical proximity data and trans-Tango results.

claims.claim: There is a parallel pathway for polarization signals in the MEDRA: DRA R7→DmDRA1, DmDRA1→MeTu, DRA R7→MeTu.
claims.source: In short, at least some MeTu neurons appear to receive input from DRA R7 photoreceptors (in addition to non-DRA photoreceptors and possibly DRA R8) and the putative connections revealed here suggest a parallel pathway for polarization signals in the MEDRA: DRA R7→DmDRA1, DmDRA1→MeTu, DRA R7→MeTu (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the connectivity data from trans-Tango and anatomical imaging.

claims.claim: Both DmDRA1 and Rh3/Rh4 trans-Tango experiments predominantly labeled the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil) of the AOTU.
claims.source: Both the DmDRA1 and Rh3/Rh4 trans-Tango experiments predominantly labeled the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil), with encroachment on the lateral domain (AOTUl) (Figure 2B''–C'').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango labeling patterns shown in Figure 2B''–C''.

claims.claim: No detectable intermediate-medial (AOTUim) or medial (AOTUm) labeling was found in either DmDRA1 or Rh3/Rh4 trans-Tango experiments.
claims.source: We found no detectable intermediate-medial (AOTUim) or medial (AOTUm) labeling in either experiment (Figure 2B'–C').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of labeling in these regions in the trans-Tango experiments.

claims.claim: There is a consistent relationship between the anterior→posterior position of MeTu dendrites in the MEDRA and the ventral→dorsal position of MeTu axon terminals in the AOTU.
claims.source: From confocal images of single-cell MCFO (MultiColor FlpOut) clones (Nern et al., 2015), we determined a consistent relationship between the anterior→posterior position of MeTu dendrites in the MEDRA and the ventral→dorsal position of MeTu axon terminals in the AOTU (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell clone data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: For MeTu neurons with dendrites outside of the MEDRA, there is no clear relationship between ventrodorsal position in the medulla and mediolateral position in the AOTU.
claims.source: For MeTu neurons with dendrites outside of the MEDRA, we found no clear relationship between ventrodorsal position in the medulla and mediolateral position in the AOTU, confirming a previous study (Timaeus et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of single-cell clones and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Both R56F07 and R73C04 MeTu populations showed a statistically significant increase in average PSI values compared to controls with the polarizer removed.
claims.source: Nonetheless, compared to control experiments with the polarizer removed, the polarizer caused a statistically significant increase in average PSI values among both MeTu populations (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The highest PSI values in R56F07 MeTu terminals were found within the most lateral regions of the population.
claims.source: In R56F07, the most responsive MeTu terminals were found within the most lateral regions of the population (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial distribution of PSI values shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In R73C04 MeTu population, the most responsive terminals tended to be clustered in a narrow medial band.
claims.source: In R73C04, the most responsive terminals tended to be clustered in a narrow medial band of the population (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), likely corresponding to the anterior region of AOTUil and possibly AOTUla.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial distribution of PSI values shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Both R56F07 and R73C04 MeTu populations showed a predominant polarotopic organization with preferred angle of polarization shifting counter-clockwise from ventral to dorsal in the right AOTU.
claims.source: Across animals, both populations showed a predominant polarotopic organization which matched our prediction: from ventral to dorsal in the right AOTU, the preferred AoP shifted counter-clockwise (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the polarotopy analysis shown in Figure 3E,F.

claims.claim: Approximately 20% of MeTu experiments showed vertical organizations of responses that deviated from the predominant polarotopy.
claims.source: However, we observed vertical organizations of responses which deviated from the norm in approximately 20% of experiments across both drivers.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the quantitative analysis of the polarotopy data across experiments.

claims.claim: The most common deviation from predominant polarotopy resembled an inverted form with clockwise rotation of preferred angle of polarization from ventral to dorsal.
claims.source: The most common of these resembled an inverted form of the predominant polarotopy (from ventral to dorsal in the right AOTU, the preferred AoP rotated clockwise) and also typically contained tunings to a different range of AoPs than the predominant organization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,E').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the alternative polarotopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,E'.

claims.claim: Distinct regions in the AOTU were modulated by either polarized or unpolarized light stimuli.
claims.source: Distinct regions could be observed which were modulated by either the polarized or unpolarized light stimuli (green or blue, respectively, Figure 4A), along with areas that were equally active during both experiments (white, Figure 4A, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined activity maps shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Lateral MeTu terminals in R73C04 showed a vertical polarotopic organization consistent with anatomical mapping.
claims.source: Within ROIs drawn on lateral MeTu terminals in R73C04 (likely occupying the ventral AOTUlc domain, green ROIs, Figure 4A, left), we found moderate modulation of activity during the rotation of the polarizer (Figure 4B) which was sufficient to identify the preferred AoP. Like the terminals with above-threshold PSI values (Figure 3D), we observed a vertical polarotopic organization consistent with the anatomical mapping of MeTu neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D): from ventral to dorsal, the AoP rotated counter-clockwise in the right AOTU and clockwise in the left AOTU (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: An intermediate band of MeTu terminals showed clear responses to bars in ipsilateral-frontal and frontal positions.
claims.source: Within an intermediate band of MeTu terminals (likely corresponding to AOTUla, blue ROIs, Figure 4A), left, we observed clear responses to bars in ipsilateral-frontal and frontal positions, with the more frontal position represented dorsally in the AOTU on both sides of the brain (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the bar response data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In the ventral AOTU, responses to bars presented in the contralateral-lateral visual field (±90° azimuth) were found, outside the field of view of the ipsilateral eye.
claims.source: In the ventral AOTU, we found responses to bars presented in the contralateral-lateral visual field (±90° azimuth), outside the field of view of the ipsilateral eye (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the bar response data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claims.claim: Retinotopic representations of both visual space and angles of polarization are found within different regions of the lateral and intermediate-lateral domains of the AOTU.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that retinotopic representations of both visual space and angles of polarization are found within different regions of the lateral and intermediate-lateral domains of the AOTU (Figure 4C,E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined polarization and bar response data.

claims.claim: MeTu neurons were stimulated by a sparse dot-field pattern simulating forward thrust optic-flow.
claims.source: Here, we found that MeTu neurons were indeed stimulated by a sparse dot-field pattern presented at different locations (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the optic-flow response data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Trans-Tango from R73C04-Gal4 MeTu neurons revealed clear labeling of a population of neurons projecting to the bulb resembling TuBu neurons.
claims.source: We found clear labeling of a population of neurons projecting to the bulb which resembled the tubercular-bulbar (TuBu) neurons (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 5A'), in addition to labeling of the inter-tubercle tract (ITT) (Strausfeld, 1976; Figure 5A''), suggesting inter-hemispheric signaling postsynaptic to MeTu neurons in the AOTU.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango labeling shown in Figure 5A'.

claims.claim: Trans-Tango from R73C04-Gal4 MeTu neurons revealed labeling of the inter-tubercle tract (ITT), suggesting inter-hemispheric signaling.
claims.source: We found clear labeling of a population of neurons projecting to the bulb which resembled the tubercular-bulbar (TuBu) neurons (Omoto et al., 2017; Figure 5A'), in addition to labeling of the inter-tubercle tract (ITT) (Strausfeld, 1976; Figure 5A''), suggesting inter-hemispheric signaling postsynaptic to MeTu neurons in the AOTU.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the trans-Tango labeling shown in Figure 5A'' and inference about function.

claims.claim: R17F12-Gal4 is expressed by a population of two tubercular-tubercle (TuTu) neurons per brain hemisphere.
claims.source: We then identified a Gal4 driver (R17F12-Gal4) that is expressed by a population of two tubercular-tubercle (TuTu) neurons per brain hemisphere, with axonal projections to the contralateral AOTU via the ITT (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical characterization shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: TuTu neurons predominantly innervate the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil) within the AOTU.
claims.source: Within the AOTU, these TuTu neurons predominantly innervate the intermediate-lateral domain (AOTUil) (Figure 5B').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5B'.

claims.claim: TuTuB neurons in the hemibrain connectome are postsynaptic to partially-reconstructed MeTu neurons in the AOTU.
claims.source: The TuTuB neurons are postsynaptic to partially-reconstructed MeTu neurons in the AOTU (MC61), corroborating our trans-Tango results (Figure 5A''), and we suggest that they likely correspond to the TuTu neurons investigated here (see Appendix 1—table 1 for correspondence between neurons in genetic drivers used and neurons in the hemibrain connectome).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the hemibrain connectome data and comparison with the genetic driver expression.

claims.claim: TuTu neurons did not show responses to unpolarized bar stimuli at any of the positions tested.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, we did not find responses to the unpolarized bar stimuli at any of the positions tested (Figure 5C), indicating that these TuTu neurons likely do not mediate the contralateral responses we observed in the MeTu neurons (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the bar response data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: TuTu neurons were polarization-sensitive with PSI values similar to those of MeTu neurons.
claims.source: Rather, we found that the TuTu neurons were polarization-sensitive with PSI values similar to those of the MeTu neurons (Figure 5E), and tunings to a limited range of polarization angles (~30°) centered around a near-horizontal orientation (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 5E and tuning data in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: TuTu neurons showed tunings to a limited range of polarization angles (~30°) centered around a near-horizontal orientation.
claims.source: Rather, we found that the TuTu neurons were polarization-sensitive with PSI values similar to those of the MeTu neurons (Figure 5E), and tunings to a limited range of polarization angles (~30°) centered around a near-horizontal orientation (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning map shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: TuBua and TuBus neurons recorded in the AOTU contained high PSI values indicating strong modulation by the polarizer.
claims.source: Among the dendrites of TuBu neurons recorded in the AOTU, we found that the populations innervating the AOTUl and AOTUil domains (TuBus and TuBua, respectively) contained high PSI values that indicated strong modulation by the polarizer (Figure 6B), with average values significantly higher than the background regions of recordings (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 6B,C.

claims.claim: TuBui dendrites innervating the AOTUim domain contained PSI values not greater than 0.5 and were indistinguishable from background regions on average.
claims.source: In contrast, dendrites innervating the AOTUim domain (TuBui) contained PSI values not greater than 0.5 (Figure 6B) and, on average, were indistinguishable from background regions (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 6B,C.

claims.claim: TuBua and TuBus dendrites showed a common relationship between preferred angle of polarization and ventral-dorsal position within the AOTU.
claims.source: Pooling data from both domains, the preferred AoP covered a range of angles from −90° to +90° and we found a common relationship between preferred AoP and ventral-dorsal position within the AOTU (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the polarotopy analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The direction of polarotopy in TuBua and TuBus dendrites matched the direction of polarotopy in the putatively presynaptic MeTu neurons.
claims.source: For the dendrites of TuBua and TuBus neurons, we found that the direction of polarotopy in the AOTU (a counter-clockwise rotation of preferred AoP from ventral to dorsal) matched the direction of polarotopy in the putatively presynaptic MeTu neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the polarotopy data from TuBu and MeTu neurons.

claims.claim: The relative positions of tunings along the ventrodorsal axis of the AOTU do not correspond directly between TuBu dendrites and MeTu terminals.
claims.source: However, the relative positions of tunings along the ventrodorsal axis of the AOTU do not correspond directly. For example, in the dorsal half of the AOTU the preferred AoPs of MeTu terminals were in the range 0° to +90° (Figure 3E,F), whereas for TuBua dendrites in the dorsal half of the AOTU preferred AoPs were in the range −90° to 0° (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the tuning ranges in MeTu and TuBu neurons.

claims.claim: The mismatch in tuning positions suggests either inhibitory input from MeTu neurons or integration of additional inputs from unidentified polarization-sensitive elements at TuBu dendrites.
claims.source: If MeTu neurons are indeed presynaptic to TuBu neurons in the AOTU, this result suggests either inhibitory input from MeTu neurons, which would effectively shift the preferred AoP by 90°, or the integration of additional inputs from unidentified polarization-sensitive elements at the dendrites of TuBu neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mismatch in tuning positions between MeTu and TuBu neurons.

claims.claim: The majority of TuBus neurons recorded in micro-glomeruli in the BUs contained low PSI values, with high PSI values interspersed among them.
claims.source: Spatial maps of PSI values revealed that the majority of TuBus neurons recorded in micro-glomeruli in the BUs contained low PSI values, and interspersed among them were micro-glomeruli with high PSI values (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI maps shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: All TuBua neurons recorded exhibited high PSI values in the BUa.
claims.source: Finally, we found that all TuBua neurons recorded exhibited high PSI values in the BUa (Figure 7A,B), in two Gal4 drivers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claims.claim: Average PSI values in the BUa were greater than 0.5 in both TuBua drivers.
claims.source: Average PSI values in the BUa were greater than 0.5 in both drivers (Figure 7C), while in the BUi and BUs, the average PSI values were not significantly different from the average in background regions of recordings, typically around 0.2 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative PSI analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: In the BUi and BUs, average PSI values were not significantly different from the average in background regions of recordings.
claims.source: Average PSI values in the BUa were greater than 0.5 in both drivers (Figure 7C), while in the BUi and BUs, the average PSI values were not significantly different from the average in background regions of recordings, typically around 0.2 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Among active pixels in both the BUs and BUa, there was a significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls, with the effect size larger in the BUa.
claims.source: Among active pixels in both the BUs and BUa we found a significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls, with the effect size larger in the latter (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Polarized light responses were found in TuBu neuron output micro-glomeruli in both the superior and anterior bulb.
claims.source: In sum, we found polarized light responses in TuBu neuron output micro-glomeruli in both the superior and anterior bulb, and no appreciable responses to polarized light in TuBu neuron outputs in the inferior bulb.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the PSI data from the three bulb regions.

claims.claim: No appreciable responses to polarized light were found in TuBu neuron outputs in the inferior bulb.
claims.source: In sum, we found polarized light responses in TuBu neuron output micro-glomeruli in both the superior and anterior bulb, and no appreciable responses to polarized light in TuBu neuron outputs in the inferior bulb.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the PSI data from the three bulb regions.

claims.claim: A cluster of micro-glomeruli toward the medial edge of the superior bulb tended to show preferential responses to similar angles of polarization.
claims.source: We observed that a cluster of micro-glomeruli toward the medial edge of the superior bulb tended to show preferential responses to similar angles of polarization (AoP) (Figure 7A, bottom).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning map shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: In the BUs, there was a non-uniform distribution of preferred angles of polarization with the highest frequency around −45° in the left bulb and +45° in the right bulb.
claims.source: When we examined the distribution of preferred AoPs in the BUs we found a non-uniform distribution with the highest frequency of preferred AoPs around −45° in the left bulb (Figure 7F) and +45° in the right bulb (Figure 7F').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the polar histograms shown in Figure 7F,F'.

claims.claim: In the anterior bulb (BUa), there was an approximately uniform representation of preferred angles of polarization in TuBua neurons.
claims.source: Conversely, in the anterior bulb (BUa) on both sides we found an approximately uniform representation of preferred AoPs in TuBua neurons (Figure 7G,G').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the polar histograms shown in Figure 7G,G'.

claims.claim: Each TuBu neuron connects exclusively with one ring neuron in the bulb.
claims.source: For the neuron populations examined here, our light microscopy images and the hemibrain connectome data (Scheffer et al., 2020) show that each TuBu neuron (BU input) connects exclusively with one ring neuron (BU output), suggesting that the distribution of preferred AoPs in the TuBu populations should be homogeneously sampled by populations of postsynaptic ring neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of light microscopy and hemibrain connectome data.

claims.claim: TuBus and TuBui neuron populations showed responses to unpolarized blue light flash in the AOTU and more strongly in the BU.
claims.source: TuBus and TuBui neuron populations showed responses to the flash in the AOTU and, more strongly, in the BU, while TuBua neurons recorded in either neuropil were inhibited by the unpolarized light stimulus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flash response data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: TuBua neurons were inhibited by unpolarized blue light flash in both the AOTU and BU.
claims.source: TuBus and TuBui neuron populations showed responses to the flash in the AOTU and, more strongly, in the BU, while TuBua neurons recorded in either neuropil were inhibited by the unpolarized light stimulus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the flash response data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: ER2 and ER4m ring neuron populations target the outer central domain of the ellipsoid body, albeit following different trajectories.
claims.source: Both ER2 and ER4m ring neuron populations target the outer central domain of the EB, albeit following different trajectories (Figure 8A,B; Omoto et al., 2018; Omoto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 8A,B and citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Only a subset of ER2 neurons in the BUs were modulated by polarized light.
claims.source: As with TuBus micro-glomerular outputs, we found that only a subset of ER2 neurons in the BUs were modulated by polarized light, with above-threshold PSI values typically in a medial cluster with a preferred angle of polarization (AoP) around 45° (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI and tuning data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Average PSI values in ER2 neurons were not significantly different from average values in background regions.
claims.source: Low PSI values were common throughout the ER2 population and average values were not significantly different from average values in background regions (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: In ER4m neurons in the BUa, average PSI values were greater than 0.5.
claims.source: By contrast, in ER4m neurons in the BUa, average PSI values were greater than 0.5 (Figure 8D) and the overall distribution of values in the population was similar in shape to the distribution in TuBua neurons (Figure 6B, Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The polarizer had a significant effect on PSI values of ER4m neurons versus controls with the polarizer removed.
claims.source: We found that the polarizer had a significant effect on PSI values of ER4m neurons versus controls with the polarizer removed (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: Individual ER4m neurons exhibited distinct preferences for angle of polarization in each recording.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that the dendrites of individual ER4m neurons exhibited distinct preferences for AoP in each recording (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning map shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: ER4m neurons almost certainly acquire their polarization-tuned responses from the presynaptic TuBua neurons in the BUa.
claims.source: Since ER4m neurons appear to receive monosynaptic input from TuBu neurons, we conclude that they almost certainly acquire their polarization-tuned responses from the presynaptic TuBua neurons in the BUa (Figure 8A,B,F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the connectivity and response properties of ER4m and TuBua neurons.

claims.claim: The average PSI value decreased from TuBua neurons to ER4m neurons.
claims.source: We note that the average PSI value decreased from TuBua neurons to ER4m neurons (Figure 8G',H', Appendix 1—figure 1B) and we further explore the transformation of their signals in the next section.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of PSI values between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claims.claim: Modulation of ER4m activity by the polarizer was observed in the ellipsoid body, indicated by their polarization-selectivity index.
claims.source: As expected from recordings in the dendritic regions of ER4m in the anterior bulb (BUa), we observed modulation of their activity with rotations of the polarizer, indicated by their polarization-selectivity index (PSI) (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: In some recordings, above-threshold PSI values in ER4m terminals were spatially localized to approximately one quadrant of the ellipsoid body.
claims.source: We noted that in some recordings, above-threshold PSI values were spatially localized to approximately one quadrant of the EB (Figure 9A,B, top, arrowhead).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI maps shown in Figure 9A,B.

claims.claim: Individual ER4m terminals exhibited tunings to distinct angles of polarization, and a range of tunings could be found intermingled at any given position in the ellipsoid body.
claims.source: Individual ER4m terminals exhibited tunings to distinct angles of polarization (AoP), and a range of tunings could be found intermingled at any given position in the EB (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning maps shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: In many recordings, the preferred angles of polarization of ER4m terminals were similar to each other and did not represent a full range of angles of polarization.
claims.source: Additionally, we found that in many recordings the preferred angles of polarization (AoPs) of terminals were similar to each other and did not represent a full range of AoPs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the tuning data across recordings.

claims.claim: The range of angles of polarization found in ER4m terminals varied across animals.
claims.source: The range of AoPs found varied across animals (Figure 9B), and as a result the frequency of preferred AoPs formed a unimodal distribution centered on a different angle in each recording (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning maps and polar histograms shown in Figure 9B,C.

claims.claim: The average activity of an entire ER4m population in the ellipsoid body exhibited modulation induced by the polarizer and a single preferred angle of polarization could be identified for each population.
claims.source: As a result of the non-uniform distributions of preferred AoPs, it followed that the average activity of an entire ER4m population in the EB exhibited modulation induced by the polarizer and a single preferred AoP could effectively be identified for each population (Figure 9D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the population response data shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: For ER4m terminals in the ellipsoid body, population tuning vectors had lengths exceeding 0.74 and an average length of 0.51 across animals.
claims.source: For ER4m terminals in the EB we found population tuning vectors with lengths exceeding 0.74 and an average length of 0.51 across animals (Figure 9E), while for ER4m dendrites recorded in either the left or right BUa individually we found an average length of 0.39 (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the population tuning vector analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: For ER4m dendrites recorded in either the left or right BUa individually, the average population tuning vector length was 0.39.
claims.source: For ER4m terminals in the EB we found population tuning vectors with lengths exceeding 0.74 and an average length of 0.51 across animals (Figure 9E), while for ER4m dendrites recorded in either the left or right BUa individually we found an average length of 0.39 (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the population tuning vector analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: For TuBua populations recorded in either bulb, the average population tuning vector length was 0.18 across animals.
claims.source: For TuBua populations recorded in either bulb we found that the vector lengths did not exceed 0.3 and the average length was 0.18 across animals (Figure 9G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the population tuning vector analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claims.claim: The increasing vector length from TuBua to ER4m in the bulb, then from ER4m dendrites in the bulb to terminals in the ellipsoid body, indicates a reduction in the range of angles of polarization found at each stage.
claims.source: This increasing vector length, first from TuBua to ER4m in the bulb, then from the dendrites of ER4m in the bulb to the terminals in the EB, indicates a reduction in the range of AoPs found at each stage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the population tuning vector analysis.

claims.claim: There is not an exact correlation between polarized light responses in the populations of presynaptic TuBua neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in an individual animal.
claims.source: These findings suggest that there is not an exact correlation between polarized light responses in the populations of presynaptic TuBua neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in an individual animal.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in tuning distributions between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claims.claim: In ER4m dendrites, the average strength of modulation is reduced compared to TuBua neurons, illustrated by the decrease in PSI values.
claims.source: In ER4m dendrites, the average strength of modulation is reduced compared to TuBua neurons, illustrated by the decrease in PSI values (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1—figure 1B), and the distribution of tunings is less uniform (Figure 9F,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of PSI values and tuning distributions between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claims.claim: The ensemble activity of ER4m synapses could convey a preferential response for a particular angle of polarization to columnar neurons at any location in the ellipsoid body.
claims.source: As a consequence, it appears that the ensemble activity of ER4m synapses could convey a preferential response for a particular angle of polarization to columnar neurons at any location in the EB.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the population response properties of ER4m neurons.

claims.claim: Ring neurons provide inhibitory input to E-PG neurons in the ellipsoid body.
claims.source: Ring neurons provide inhibitory input to E-PG neurons in the EB (Figure 10A), where interactions between ring and E-PG neurons are thought to be reciprocal (Fisher et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Omoto et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on ring neuron and E-PG connectivity.

claims.claim: Interactions between ring neurons and E-PG neurons in the ellipsoid body are thought to be reciprocal.
claims.source: Ring neurons provide inhibitory input to E-PG neurons in the EB (Figure 10A), where interactions between ring and E-PG neurons are thought to be reciprocal (Fisher et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Omoto et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on central complex connectivity.

claims.claim: Connectivity between presynaptic E-PG neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in the ellipsoid body was confirmed using activity-dependent GRASP.
claims.source: We confirmed connectivity between presynaptic E-PG neurons and postsynaptic ER4m neurons in the EB in the genetic drivers used (ER4m: R34D03-LexA, Figure 8B; E-PG: SS00096-Gal4, Figure 10—figure supplement 1A) by labeling synapses using activity-dependent GRASP (Macpherson et al., 2015; Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the GRASP data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: E-PG activity in the protocerebral bridge was modulated as the angle of polarization rotated.
claims.source: We found that E-PG activity in the PB was indeed modulated as the angle of polarization (AoP) rotated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the calcium imaging data from E-PG neurons.

claims.claim: PSI values and preferred angles of polarization in E-PG neurons showed a bilateral coupling, with the right half of the protocerebral bridge resembling the left half.
claims.source: As expected, the PSI values and preferred AoPs showed a bilateral coupling, with the right half of the PB (1R to 8R) resembling the left half (8L to 1L) (Figure 10B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI and tuning maps shown in Figure 10B,C.

claims.claim: The distribution of PSI values in E-PG neurons was not homogenous across the protocerebral bridge, with high values typically clustering across a contiguous subset of 2–4 glomeruli.
claims.source: We observed that the distribution of PSI values was not homogenous across the PB, and high values typically clustered across a contiguous subset of 2–4 glomeruli, while low PSI values occurred throughout the remaining glomeruli (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI maps shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: In each animal, the preferred angle of polarization was similar across the glomeruli in each cluster of high PSI values.
claims.source: In each animal, the preferred AoP was similar across the glomeruli in each cluster (Figure 10C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tuning maps shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: Overall, substantially lower PSI values were found in E-PG neurons than in ER4m neurons.
claims.source: Overall, we found substantially lower PSI values in E-PG neurons than in ER4m neurons (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the PSI distribution comparison shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: A statistically significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls was found in both E-PG and ER4m populations.
claims.source: We found a statistically significant effect of the polarizer on PSI values versus controls in both populations (Figure 10E), yet the effect size was small in E-PG neurons with an average ΔPSI of 0.06, and an average PSI value that was generally lower than in background regions of recordings (Appendix 1–figure 1).

claims.claim: The amplitude of responses in E-PG neurons was often found to be inconsistent over multiple rotation cycles of the polarizer.
claims.source: Here, in the PB, we observed characteristics which distinguished E-PG responses from those of all other polarization-sensitive elements that we recorded in the upstream pathway. First, the amplitude of responses was often found to be inconsistent over multiple rotation cycles of the polarizer (arrowhead, Figure 10F, top).

claims.claim: The peak response in E-PG neurons was often found to occur at different positions of the polarizer over multiple cycles.

claims.claim: Variations in response amplitude and peak position were synchronized across the left and right protocerebral bridge glomerulus pair.
claims.source: For both of these response characteristics, variations were synchronized across the left and right PB glomerulus pair (Figure 10F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the paired glomerulus response data shown in Figure 10F.

claims.claim: PSI values and preferred angles of polarization in E-PG neurons varied over time when analyzed for individual cycles of the polarizer.
claims.source: When we analyzed responses to individual cycles of the polarizer separately, these characteristics manifested as PSI values and preferred AoPs which varied over time (Figure 10G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the cycle-by-cycle analysis shown in Figure 10G.

claims.claim: Less than half of all E-PG glomeruli recorded exhibited a periodicity that matched the stimulus.
claims.source: For E-PG neurons, we found that less than half of all glomeruli recorded exhibited a periodicity which matched the stimulus, while almost all ER4m and TuBua neurons matched the stimulus (E-PG: 43.3%, ER4m: 98.4%, TuBua: 100%) (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).

claims.claim: Almost all ER4m and TuBua neurons exhibited a periodicity that matched the stimulus.
claims.source: For E-PG neurons, we found that less than half of all glomeruli recorded exhibited a periodicity which matched the stimulus, while almost all ER4m and TuBua neurons matched the stimulus (E-PG: 43.3%, ER4m: 98.4%, TuBua: 100%) (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the auto-correlation analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Across different animals, glomeruli at corresponding positions in the protocerebral bridge exhibited different preferred angles of polarization.
claims.source: Across different animals, glomeruli at corresponding positions in the PB exhibited different preferred angles of polarization (AoPs) (Figure 10C).

claims.claim: There was no common relationship between glomerulus position in the protocerebral bridge and the preferred angles of polarization of E-PG neurons across animals.

claims.claim: Glomeruli neighboring the glomerulus with the highest PSI value (G0) at ±1 protocerebral bridge position were likely to exhibit a similar preferred angle of polarization to G0, to within 15°.

claims.source: At ±2–4 PB positions from G0, we found preferred AoPs generally shifted toward orthogonal angles (Figure 10I, Figure 10—figure supplement 1F,G) and among these positions there was again a similarity between neighboring glomeruli (Figure 10—figure supplement 1H).

claims.claim: The encoding of polarization information in E-PG neurons could be viewed as a limited representation of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization.
claims.source: Simplistically, this could be viewed as a limited representation of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization among E-PG neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the tuning data from E-PG neurons.

claims.claim: Each section of the Drosophila anterior visual pathway contains polarization-tuned neurons.
claims.source: In this study, we have demonstrated that each section of the Drosophila anterior visual pathway (AVP) contains polarization-tuned neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The anterior visual pathway neurons provide a circuit to convey polarized light signals from the dorsal rim area of the eye to the compass neurons of the central complex, via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb.
claims.source: Together, they provide a circuit to convey polarized light signals from the specialized dorsal rim area of the eye to the compass neurons of the central complex, via the anterior optic tubercle and bulb.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the connectivity and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The anterior visual pathway also conveys information about unpolarized visual features.
claims.source: This pathway also conveys information about unpolarized visual features, as shown here and in previous studies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the bar and optic-flow response data in the current study and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The encoding of multiple visual modalities, similarities in constituent neurons, and organization of neuropils support the view that the anterior visual pathway in Drosophila is homologous to the sky compass pathway described in other insects.
claims.source: The encoding of multiple visual modalities, the similarities in the constituent neurons, and the organization of the neuropils which accommodate them (Omoto et al., 2017), support the view that the AVP in Drosophila is homologous to the sky compass pathway described in locusts, bees, butterflies, and beetles, among other insects (Honkanen et al., 2019; Warren et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the current findings and comparison with other insects, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Almost the full extent of the dorsal rim area was stimulated by polarized light originating from a single point in the visual field with a common angle of polarization.
claims.source: Surprisingly, almost the full extent of the DRA was stimulated by polarized light originating from a single point in the visual field with a common angle of polarization.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the observation that a wide range of polarization tunings was revealed in downstream neurons despite the stimulus configuration.

claims.claim: The Drosophila medulla dorsal rim area analyzes the overall pattern of polarized light in the sky and extracts a predominant angle of polarization.
claims.source: A wide range of polarization tunings was subsequently revealed in downstream neurons, supporting the idea that the Drosophila medulla dorsal rim area (MEDRA) analyzes the overall pattern of polarized light in the sky and extracts a predominant angle of polarization (AoP) (Labhart, 2016; Rossel and Wehner, 1986), rather than performing many local AoP estimates.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the response properties of downstream neurons and citations to previous theoretical work.

claims.claim: During the morning and evening when D. melanogaster are most active, the pattern of polarization in the sky can be well approximated by a single, predominant angle of polarization.
claims.source: During the morning and evening when D. melanogaster are most active, the pattern of polarization in the sky can be well approximated by a single, predominant AoP.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the natural polarization patterns during Drosophila activity periods, based on knowledge of atmospheric optics.

claims.claim: DmDRA1 neurons spatially integrate polarization signals from multiple columns of the MEDRA.
claims.source: DmDRA1 neurons appear to spatially integrate polarization signals from multiple columns of the MEDRA (Figure 1), and individual neurons heavily overlap each other (Sancer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the anatomical properties of DmDRA1 neurons and their response properties.

claims.claim: Spatial integration by DmDRA1 neurons could provide robustness to occlusions of the sky or of the dorsal rim area itself and average out inconsistencies in the available light.
claims.source: This could provide an additional robustness to occlusions of the sky or of the DRA itself and average out inconsistencies in the available light (Labhart et al., 2001; Rossel and Wehner, 1986).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional benefit of spatial integration, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The parallel circuitry between DRA R7, DmDRA1, and MeTu neurons in MEDRA columns resembles the color-processing pathway found in non-DRA columns involving R7, Dm8, and Tm5c.
claims.source: The parallel circuitry between DRA R7, DmDRA1, and MeTu neurons in MEDRA columns (Figure 2D), resembles the color-processing pathway found in non-DRA columns involving R7, Dm8, and Tm5c (Gao et al., 2008; Karuppudurai et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of circuit motifs based on anatomical and functional similarities, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Color and polarization processing are compatible in MeTu neurons.
claims.source: MeTu neurons in the MEDRA may also integrate color signals, as their dendritic fields extend into the non-DRA medulla, indicating that color and polarization processing are compatible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical properties of MeTu neurons.

claims.claim: The AOTU in Drosophila is likely to be a site for modulation of signals depending on time or internal states.
claims.source: The AOTU in Drosophila is also likely to be a site for modulation of signals depending on time or internal states (el Jundi et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2018; Lamaze et al., 2018), and a capacity to modify responses may explain why we observed multiple polarotopic organizations in a MeTu neuron population in the AOTU (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on citations to previous research and the observation of variable polarotopy.

claims.claim: TuBu neurons extract a processed form of the signals in the AOTU, encoding visual features within fewer neurons than the MeTu populations.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that TuBu neurons extract a processed form of the signals in the AOTU, encoding visual features within fewer neurons than the MeTu populations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of tuning properties and neuron numbers between MeTu and TuBu populations.

claims.claim: TuBu neurons appear to divide signals into functional groups.
claims.source: TuBu neurons appear to divide signals into functional groups, and the anterior bulb-projecting TuBua group in every fly contained a set of around six tunings covering −90° to +90° of polarization space in approximately 30° steps, tightly packed in a micro-glomerular structure with no apparent polarotopy (Figure 7, Figure 8).

claims.claim: The site of integration of celestial cues is not at the synapse between TuBu and ring neurons.
claims.source: Hence, we posit that the site of integration of celestial cues is not at the synapse between TuBu and ring neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the one-to-one connectivity between TuBu and ring neurons.

claims.claim: The populations of TuBus neurons recorded contained a limited range of tunings and resembled a system for detecting visual features with a particular polarization signature.
claims.source: Although we found evidence that angles of polarization are represented in the superior bulb (Figure 7, Figure 8), where unpolarized cues are also known to be represented, the populations we recorded contained a limited range of tunings and resembled a system for detecting visual features with a particular polarization signature (Labhart, 2016), such as horizontally polarized light reflected from surfaces like water, rather than a system for accurate estimation of orientation.

claims.claim: ER4m ring neurons do not simply relay the responses of presynaptic TuBua neurons to the ellipsoid body.
claims.source: By recording the ensemble response of a population of ER4m ring neurons, both in the anterior bulb and ellipsoid body (EB), we determined that they do not simply relay the responses of presynaptic TuBua neurons to the EB.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in response properties between TuBua and ER4m neurons.

claims.claim: ER4m ring neurons appear to deliver a subset of signals more prominently than others, bestowing the population with an ensemble response tuned to a specific angle of polarization.
claims.source: Instead, they appear to deliver a subset of signals more prominently than others, bestowing the population with an ensemble response tuned to a specific angle of polarization (Figure 9).

claims.source: Furthermore, we found that this population tuning conveys a different angle of polarization in individual animals, and one exciting possibility is that this represents a flexible heading signal relative to polarized light cues, which could direct behavior (Warren et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Among ER4m and E-PG neurons, polarization tunings are not represented with a retinotopic map in the ellipsoid body or protocerebral bridge which is common between individual animals.

claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies in locusts, supported by citations.

claims.claim: E-PG neurons may respond to one of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization, effectively dividing the population into two groups.
claims.source: Our data suggest that in a given fly, E-PG neurons may respond to one of two approximately orthogonal angles of polarization, effectively dividing the population into two groups.

claims.claim: A binary system of two orthogonal preferred angles would be well suited to influence downstream processes in a motor-centered coordinate frame.
claims.source: A binary system such as this would be well suited to influence downstream processes in a motor-centered coordinate frame (Rayshubskiy et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the binary tuning system, supported by a citation.

claims.source: For example, the eventual output of the compass network may be a command signal to activate one descending neuron of a bilateral pair to initiate a turn to either the left or right, and thus maintain a heading specified by polarization patterns in the sky.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, intensity gradients have been shown to have a greater behavioral significance than polarized light.

results.result: DmDRA1 neurons in the medulla dorsal rim area (MEDRA) are polarization-sensitive, receiving input from DRA R7 photoreceptors. These neurons exhibit polarotopic organization with preferred angles of polarization shifting counter-clockwise from anterior to posterior in the right optic lobe, matching R8 photoreceptor tunings. DmDRA1 neurons show polarization opponency with excitation at preferred angles and inhibition at orthogonal angles and unpolarized light.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C44 are well-supported by calcium imaging data (Figures 1C-H), anatomical characterization (Figure 1B), and control experiments with polarizer removed (Figure 1E-F). The polarotopic organization is demonstrated with strong statistical correlations (ρ=0.85, p<10^-4), and PSI values show significant modulation (average 0.74 vs 0.20 background). The inference that R7 provides predominant input is supported by anatomical overlap, cited connectivity data, and the 90° shift expected from inhibitory photoreceptors.

results.result: MeTu neurons receive polarization signals from DRA R7 photoreceptors both directly and via DmDRA1 neurons, forming a parallel pathway in the MEDRA. Trans-Tango tracing from DmDRA1 and Rh3/Rh4 photoreceptors labels MeTu neurons projecting to the intermediate-lateral domain of the AOTU. Single-cell clones reveal a consistent mapping from anterior-posterior position in MEDRA to ventral-dorsal position in AOTU.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C57 are supported by trans-Tango connectivity data (Figure 2B-C), anatomical proximity analysis (Figure 2—supplement 1A), and single-cell MCFO clones (Figure 2E, supplement 1B-D). The parallel pathway inference is reasonable given the anatomical overlap and connectivity patterns. However, the trans-Tango technique labels putative connections that would ideally be confirmed with electrophysiology or more direct connectivity methods.

results.result: MeTu neuron populations (R56F07 and R73C04) show statistically significant polarization sensitivity in the AOTU with spatially restricted high PSI values. Both populations exhibit predominant polarotopic organization with counter-clockwise shift in preferred angle from ventral to dorsal in the right AOTU, though approximately 20% of experiments showed alternative organizations including inverted polarotopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 are supported by calcium imaging data showing significant PSI increases vs controls (Figure 2G), spatial PSI distributions (Figure 3A-B), and polarotopy analysis with significant correlations (R56F07: ρ=0.71, R73C04: ρ=0.56, p<10^-4). The observation of alternative polarotopic organizations in ~20% of experiments is documented but not fully explained, suggesting either biological variability or technical factors that warrant further investigation.

results.result: The AOTU contains functionally segregated regions encoding polarized light, unpolarized bar stimuli, and optic flow. Lateral MeTu terminals show vertical polarotopic organization, while intermediate regions respond to bars with retinotopic mapping. Responses to contralateral visual field stimuli suggest inter-hemispheric processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 are supported by combined activity maps (Figure 4A), tuning data for polarization (Figure 4B-C), bar responses (Figure 4D-E), and optic flow responses (Figure 4F). The retinotopic and polarotopic organizations are demonstrated with appropriate spatial analysis. The inference about inter-hemispheric processing from contralateral responses is reasonable but would benefit from additional circuit tracing.

results.result: TuTu neurons project via the inter-tubercle tract to the contralateral AOTU, predominantly innervating the intermediate-lateral domain. These neurons are polarization-sensitive with PSI values similar to MeTu neurons but show tunings to a limited range (~30°) centered around horizontal orientation. TuTu neurons do not respond to unpolarized bar stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C77 are supported by trans-Tango labeling (Figure 5A), anatomical characterization (Figure 5B), lack of bar responses (Figure 5C), and polarization tuning data (Figure 5E-F). The correspondence with hemibrain connectome TuTuB neurons strengthens the anatomical claims. However, the functional role of these neurons remains unclear given their limited tuning range and lack of bar responses.

results.result: TuBu neuron dendrites in the AOTU show domain-specific polarization sensitivity: TuBua and TuBus (innervating AOTUil and AOTUl) have high PSI values and common polarotopic organization, while TuBui (innervating AOTUim) shows no significant polarization sensitivity. The polarotopy direction matches MeTu neurons but with shifted tuning positions along the ventrodorsal axis, suggesting either inhibitory input or integration of additional polarization-sensitive inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 are supported by PSI analysis (Figure 6B-C) and polarotopy data (Figure 6G-I). The domain-specific differences are clear and statistically significant. The mismatch in tuning positions between MeTu and TuBu is well-documented (Figure 6I vs Figure 3E-F), and the proposed explanations (inhibitory input or additional inputs) are reasonable inferences, though direct evidence for either mechanism is not provided.

results.result: In the bulb, TuBu neuron outputs show region-specific polarization sensitivity: TuBua neurons in the anterior bulb (BUa) uniformly exhibit high PSI values (>0.5) with approximately uniform representation of preferred angles; TuBus neurons in the superior bulb (BUs) show mixed PSI values with non-uniform distribution favoring ±45°; TuBui neurons in the inferior bulb (BUi) show no appreciable polarization responses. Each TuBu neuron connects exclusively with one ring neuron.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C94 are supported by PSI spatial maps (Figure 7A), quantitative PSI analysis (Figure 7C), statistical comparisons (Figure 7E), and polar histograms (Figure 7F-G). The one-to-one connectivity with ring neurons is supported by light microscopy and hemibrain connectome data. The functional interpretation that BUa provides uniform polarization representation while BUs may detect specific polarization features is reasonable given the data.

results.result: TuBu neuron populations show differential responses to unpolarized blue light: TuBus and TuBui are excited in both AOTU and bulb (more strongly in bulb), while TuBua neurons are inhibited in both regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are supported by flash response data (Figure 7—supplement 1B). The differential responses across TuBu subtypes are clear and consistent. This provides important context for understanding how these neurons integrate polarized and unpolarized visual information.

results.result: Ring neurons ER2 and ER4m receive polarization signals in the bulb with different response properties: only a subset of ER2 neurons in BUs show polarization sensitivity, while ER4m neurons in BUa consistently show high PSI values (>0.5) with individual neurons exhibiting distinct angle preferences. ER4m neurons almost certainly acquire polarization-tuned responses from presynaptic TuBua neurons, though average PSI decreases from TuBua to ER4m.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C104 are supported by PSI analysis (Figure 8C-D), statistical comparisons (Figure 8E), tuning maps (Figure 8G), and GRASP connectivity data (Figure 8F). The inference that ER4m acquires responses from TuBua is well-supported by connectivity and response similarity. The PSI decrease suggests signal transformation, though the mechanism is not determined.

results.result: ER4m ring neuron terminals in the ellipsoid body show polarization modulation with spatially localized high PSI regions. Individual terminals exhibit distinct angle preferences, but within each animal, preferred angles are similar and form unimodal distributions centered on different angles across animals. Population tuning vectors increase in length from TuBua (0.18) to ER4m dendrites (0.39) to ER4m terminals (0.51), indicating progressive reduction in the range of angles represented. This suggests ER4m populations deliver a preferential response to a specific angle that varies across individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C117 are supported by PSI maps (Figure 9A), tuning maps (Figure 9B), polar histograms (Figure 9C), population responses (Figure 9D), and population tuning vector analysis (Figure 9E-G). The progressive increase in vector length is well-documented and statistically significant. The interpretation that this represents a flexible, animal-specific heading signal is reasonable but speculative, as the functional significance is not directly tested.

results.result: E-PG compass neurons in the protocerebral bridge show polarization modulation but with substantially lower PSI values than ER4m neurons and unique response characteristics. PSI values cluster in 2-4 contiguous glomeruli with similar preferred angles, showing bilateral coupling. E-PG responses show inconsistent amplitude and peak position across polarizer rotation cycles, with less than half of glomeruli exhibiting periodicity matching the stimulus (43.3% vs 98.4% for ER4m and 100% for TuBua).
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C132 are supported by GRASP connectivity (Figure 10—supplement 1B), PSI analysis (Figure 10B-E), time-series data (Figure 10F-G), and auto-correlation analysis (Figure 10—supplement 1C). The low PSI values and variable responses are well-documented. However, the small effect size (ΔPSI=0.06) and PSI values often lower than background raise questions about the biological significance of these responses. The interpretation that this reflects flexible encoding is reasonable but the data could also reflect weak or inconsistent polarization sensitivity.

results.result: E-PG neurons show no common polarotopic organization across animals, with glomeruli at corresponding positions exhibiting different preferred angles. However, within individual animals, neighboring glomeruli (±1 position from highest PSI) show similar tunings (within 15°), while glomeruli at ±2-4 positions shift toward orthogonal angles. This can be viewed as a limited representation of two approximately orthogonal angles.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 are supported by tuning maps across animals (Figure 10C), scatter plot analysis (Figure 10H), and tuning shift analysis (Figure 10I, supplement 1F-H). The lack of common organization matches findings in locust CL1a neurons (cited). The local organization within animals is demonstrated, though the interpretation as a binary orthogonal system is somewhat speculative and would benefit from additional analysis or modeling.

results.result: Background on insect polarization vision: Many insects use skylight polarization patterns for navigation. The dorsal rim area is a specialized eye region for detecting skylight polarization. Drosophila have been shown behaviorally to orient relative to polarization patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13, C14, C21, C22 represent well-established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to previous literature. These provide appropriate context for the current study.

results.result: Background on central complex function and sky compass pathways: The central complex in flies coordinates spatial memory, navigation, and homeostatic processes. It encodes heading direction that can be updated by proprioceptive and external cues. In other insects, the sky compass pathway transmits polarization signals from eyes to central complex. The anterior visual pathway in Drosophila has been postulated as the homologue, but polarization-processing neurons beyond the dorsal rim area had not been identified prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C20 represent established background from cited literature and appropriately frame the knowledge gap addressed by the current study. The citations support the claims about central complex function and sky compass pathways in other insects.

results.result: Main conclusion: Polarization-tuned neurons are found throughout the anterior visual pathway in Drosophila, connecting the optic lobes to the central complex via the AOTU and bulb. This pathway also conveys unpolarized visual features. The organization is homologous to sky compass pathways in other insects, with a transformation from consistent polarotopic organization in the periphery to reduced, flexible representation in the central brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C138-C141 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the comprehensive anatomical and functional data presented throughout the manuscript. The homology claim is supported by similarities in anatomy, connectivity, and function, though some differences from other insects (e.g., lack of fixed polarotopy in E-PG) are also noted.

results.result: Interpretation of MEDRA function: Almost the full extent of the DRA was stimulated by a single-point polarized light source, revealing a wide range of tunings in downstream neurons. This supports the idea that the MEDRA analyzes the overall sky polarization pattern to extract a predominant angle, rather than performing local estimates. DmDRA1 spatial integration could provide robustness to occlusions.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 are reasonable interpretations of the data, supported by the observation that a single stimulus point activated neurons with diverse tunings (Figure 1—supplement 1E-F) and the anatomical properties of DmDRA1 neurons spanning ~10 columns. The interpretation is consistent with cited theoretical work on polarization vision, though direct evidence for the proposed functional benefits is not provided.

results.result: Interpretations of circuit organization and function: The parallel circuitry in MEDRA resembles color-processing pathways. The AOTU may be a site for signal modulation. TuBu neurons extract processed signals and divide them into functional groups. The site of celestial cue integration is not at the TuBu-ring neuron synapse. TuBus neurons may detect specific polarization features rather than accurately estimate orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C147, C149-C154 represent interpretations and inferences about circuit function that are reasonable given the data but lack direct experimental support. The comparison to color pathways is based on anatomical similarity. The proposed functional roles are speculative and would require additional experiments (e.g., behavioral assays, optogenetic manipulation) to confirm.

results.result: Interpretation of ER4m function: ER4m ring neurons do not simply relay TuBua responses but deliver a subset of signals more prominently, bestowing the population with an ensemble response tuned to a specific angle that varies across animals. This may represent a flexible heading signal relative to polarized light cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C157 are interpretations of the population tuning data (Figure 9) that are reasonable but speculative. The observation that population tuning varies across animals is well-documented, but the interpretation that this represents a flexible heading signal is not directly tested. Alternative explanations (e.g., developmental variability, rearing conditions) are not ruled out.

results.result: Interpretations of E-PG responses: Polarization tunings in ER4m and E-PG neurons are not represented with a common retinotopic map across animals, matching findings for unpolarized stimuli and locust CL1a neurons. E-PG neurons may respond to one of two orthogonal angles, dividing the population into two groups suited for motor-centered processing. The lack of an activity bump is attributed to open-loop stimulation in immobilized animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C164 are interpretations that are reasonable given the data and consistent with cited literature, but remain speculative. The binary orthogonal system interpretation (C161-C163) is an interesting hypothesis but not rigorously tested. The explanation for lack of activity bump (C164) is plausible but the flexible encoding interpretation is based on variable responses that could have alternative explanations.

results.result: Context for behavioral significance: In ants and beetles, polarization cues can dominate over other visual features in navigation. In Drosophila, intensity gradients have greater behavioral significance than polarized light, yet connectome analysis suggests polarization-sensitive ring neurons may be at the top of a sensory input hierarchy.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C167 are supported by citations to behavioral studies and connectome analysis. This provides important context for interpreting the functional significance of the identified pathway, though it also highlights an apparent discrepancy between circuit organization and behavioral importance that warrants further investigation.
